hints.title: Check the original domain and each transition
hints.body: Keep the stated angle interval and the inputs where tangent is defined. For each adjacent pair of lines, check whether the written operation preserves the same permitted solutions.
hints.recap: Equations claimed to be equivalent must have the same solution set within the original domain.
hints.pitfall: A later lost restriction does not establish which error happened first.
hints.pause: List the domain restrictions and audit the transitions in their written order.

recall.reminder: Equations claimed to be equivalent must have the same solution set within the original domain.

hints.title: Separate an identity from a rule about solutions
hints.body: Expand a claimed factorisation to check its identity. For a rule that then extracts separate equations from a relation, first test that rule with ordinary real numbers. You can also compare adjacent lines at an allowed angle of your own choosing.
hints.recap: An algebraic rewriting and a claim about its solutions require separate checks.
hints.pitfall: A final candidate must still satisfy the original equation; an undefined tangent value cannot be used as a test input.

recall.reminder: An algebraic rewriting and a claim about its solutions require separate checks.

solution:
1. Validate I and II. I merely subtracts 2sinx. Expanding II gives sinxtanx−sinx−cosxtanx+cosx. Since cosxtanx=sinx on the original domain, this is the expression in I.

2. Inspect III. A product of real numbers equal to −1 does not force either factor to equal −1. The zero-product rule cannot be used here.

3. Confirm the lost equivalence. x=0 satisfies III but fails II and the original equation.

Answer D: the first error is on line III. Later issues do not change which error occurs first.
knowledgePattern: Find the first misuse of factor reasoning in a trigonometric solution
